analysis: While F1c cut the leader from its followers, orchestrators and etcd (not from the gateways), COMMITs on the leader waited for a synchronous standby. When a client gave up after P01 (10 s; completion info, §6.2 row 9), the pooler cancelled the backend's statement on context end (go/services/multipooler/internal/pools/regular/regular_conn.go execWithContextCancel → handleContextCancellation); PostgreSQL ends a cancelled synchronous-replication wait by completing the commit locally (S61: 'The transaction has already committed locally, but might not have been replicated'). Other sessions on the old leader then read the unacknowledged values (ok reads). After multiorch failed over to a follower that never received them, the old leader was rewound and the values disappeared: two ok reads of one key are not prefixes of each other (C3 incompatible-order). No ok write is missing from the final reads (C1 valid) and no failed write is visible (C2 valid).

completion_review.row_reason: client timeout after a write was sent (the write whose value later vanished)

harness_review: §6.2 review: every reviewed completion matches its recorded err and row (reads ok, row 1; the writes of the vanished values info, row 9: the client's P01 deadline expired after the write was sent). A misclassification could hide or invent this anomaly only if an ok read were not a successful read or a vanished value came from an ok/fail write; neither holds. Every fault of the run was confirmed and healed (run-end complete); the anomaly is between ok reads of the real build's history; the minimized plan reproduces it (REPRODUCED).
known_status_reasoning: No match among the alpha-known-gap issues named in RESEARCH S50 (#1059 prune unhealthy cohort members, #1060 problem code when failover is unsafe); the contents of #1065 and #1126–#1128 are not in the research register, so a match there is not excluded. Nothing was looked up online (AGENTS.md §6).

oracle.triage: elle-cli (validity, process and realtime passes, cpcheck --elle-oracle) also judges the history invalid and also reports incompatible-order on key 13, and in addition a G-single cycle (and G-single-realtime) whose anti-dependency edge starts at the read (t = 20.75 s) that observed value 35 — the unacknowledged write that later vanished. Adya's cycle classes presuppose one version order per object (S72); the reads of key 13 admit none (incompatible order), so an edge derived from that read depends on the order a tool chooses. CONTRACT §10.3 defines C3's order as the longest read and reports non-prefix reads as incompatible-order; by that definition the history's class is incompatible-order and neither tool is wrong about validity. Labelled oracle-disagreement (§10.11); no checker change (K4 forbids checker changes without a K2 case; this is not a C3 defect by §10.3). LIMITATIONS: C3 does not derive cycles through keys whose reads are incompatible.

origin_reasoning: The visibility of a commit whose synchronous-replication wait was cancelled is documented PostgreSQL behavior (S61); the cancel is issued by Multigres' pooler when the request context ends, and the loss follows from a Multigres failover. Not reproduced on plain PostgreSQL streaming replication (R15), so the origin hypothesis is UNDETERMINED.
